newsitem.title: GREECE: GREECE SAYS BRITISH COMMENTS ON CYPRUS UNJUST.
newsitem.headline: GREECE SAYS BRITISH COMMENTS ON CYPRUS UNJUST.

text.p: Greece said on Tuesday comments by British Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind on the possibility of war breaking out between Greece and Turkey over Cyprus were unjust and it blamed Ankara for the tension.

"The suggestions should be addressed to Turkey which has an occupation force on Cyprus, it violates our airspace and threatens to use force in the Aegean in violation of international law," Press and Information Minister Dimitris Reppas told reporters.
Rifkind, speaking on BBC radio earlier on Tuesday, accused Athens and Ankara of lacking the political will to find a solution.
"When relations are already bad and tense and difficult and both sides appear to be looking for an excuse to make them worse, that is pretty grim," he said.
Asked whether there might be conflict between Greece and Turkey in the Aegean, Rifkind said: "It has to be a serious possibility."
"I am not as confident as logic would imply because there has been a real lack of political will on both sides," he added.
Reppas said Greece had expressed its political will for calm and that Ankara should accept a proposal by Nicosia and Athens for a demilitarised Cyprus.
"Greece and Turkey should not by judged equally by analysts and international figures. Greece is a European Union member which abides by international law," he said.

The United States and Britain expressed alarm last month over a Greek Cypriot decision to buy Russian surface-to-air missiles, saying it could destabilise what is already one of the most heavily militarised areas of the world.
On a visit to the divided island in December, Rifkind told Greek Cypriot leaders the planned purchase would be a "big step in the wrong direction."

The planned acquisition of the S-300 system would neutralise the air superiority Turkey has had since 1974 when its troops invaded the northern third of Cyprus in response to a short-lived coup engineered by the military then ruling Greece.
Tension has increased perceptibly on the island in the past six months after the deaths of four people in ceasefire line incidents and both sides continue to build up their defences.
